content:
I am running a research project comparing real-world stories with decision situations. I will give you descriptions of four games and two short stories.

INSTRUCTIONS

Below are four games (A, B, C, D) and two stories (Story 1, Story 2).

For each of the 8 story x game pairs, rate how similar the two situations are in their underlying decision structure on a 0-100 scale:

0 = the situations have no meaningful similarity in their underlying decision structure

100 = the situations have essentially the same underlying decision structure

Assess each pair independently and base your judgment only on the descriptions provided. Use your own judgment to decide which aspects of the situations are relevant and how much weight to give them. Apply the same standard across all eight pairs. Equal ratings are allowed, and the ratings do not need to sum to any particular total.

OUTPUT FORMAT

1. For each of the 8 pairs, give the rating and a 2-3 sentence justification identifying the main considerations behind the rating.

2. At the end, output a single JSON object with the 8 ratings, exactly in this form:
{"ratings": {"A": {"Story 1": <0-100>, "Story 2": <0-100>}, "B": {...}, "C": {...}, "D": {...}}}

3. After the JSON, briefly identify the most and least similar game or games for each story and explain why. Allow for ties.

--- GAME A ---

In this task, you are matched with another Prolific participant. You
will never know the identity of the person with whom you are paired, and
this person will never know your identity. One of you will be assigned
to be Player 1, and the other will be assigned to be Player 2.

Player 1 will receive $6, and Player 2 will receive $0. Player 1 will
decide how much of the $6 to send to Player 2. Any amount sent will be
multiplied by 3 before being received by Player 2.

After receiving this amount, Player 2 will decide how much of it to send
back to Player 1. The amount sent back will not be changed.

The final allocation will be implemented for 1 participant out of 10.
This means that your decision affects a bonus payment you and the other
participant may receive.

[On the next screen, Player 1 sees:]

Please choose how much of the $6 you would like to send to Player 2.
The remaining amount will be yours.

Any amount you send will be multiplied by 3 before being received by
Player 2.

Player 2 will then decide how much of the amount received to send back
to you.
--- GAME B ---

In this task, you are matched with another Prolific participant. You
will never know the identity of the person with whom you are paired, and
this person will never know your identity. One of you will be assigned
to be Player 1, and the other will be assigned to be Player 2.

Player 1 is provisionally allocated $12. Player 1 will have the chance
to decide whether and how to change this original allocation.

After seeing the proposed allocation, Player 2 will decide whether to
accept or reject it. If Player 2 accepts, the proposed allocation will
be implemented. If Player 2 rejects, both players will receive $0.

The final allocation will be implemented for 1 participant out of 10.
This means that your decision affects a bonus payment you and the other
participant may receive.

[On the next screen, Player 1 sees:]

Please choose how much of the $12 you would like to transfer to Player
2.

If the transfer is accepted, it will be implemented.
--- GAME C ---

Allocation Task - Instructions

In this task, you are matched with another Prolific participant. You
will never know the identity of the person with whom you are paired, and
this person will never know your identity. You and your match are
provisionally allocated a certain amount of dollars, adding to a total
of $12. You will have the chance to decide whether and how to change
this original allocation.

The allocation chosen will be implemented for 1 participant out of 10.
This means that your decisions affect a bonus payment you and the other
participant may receive. It is thus in your best interest to choose the
allocations that you truly prefer.

[On the next screen, the participant sees:]

You were provisionally allocated $8. The other participant was
provisionally allocated $4.

You can transfer any amount between -$4 and $8. If you choose a
negative dollar transfer to the other participant, this means that you
take that amount from the other participant.
--- GAME D ---

Allocation Task - Instructions

In this task, you are matched with another Prolific participant. You
will never know the identity of the person with whom you are paired, and
this person will never know your identity. You and your match are
provisionally allocated a certain amount of dollars, adding to a total
of $12. You will have the chance to decide whether and how to change
this original allocation.

The allocation chosen will be implemented for 1 participant out of 10.
This means that your decisions affect a bonus payment you and the other
participant may receive. It is thus in your best interest to choose the
allocations that you truly prefer.

[On the next screen, the participant sees:]

You were provisionally allocated $12. The other participant was
provisionally allocated $0.

You have the option to make a transfer to the other participant. You can
transfer any amount between $0 and $12.
--- STORY 1 ---

James was going through a rough financial patch. He struggled to make
ends meet and had no savings left. One morning, he received an
unexpected email from a government welfare agency he had applied to
months ago. "Congratulations! You have been selected for financial
assistance. You will be receiving the full aid amount to help with your
expenses." As James went to the agency to collect, he found Mark, a
neighbor. He learned that Mark also applied but wasn't selected. Only
James received the funds. Now James faced a choice. Should he keep all
the money for himself? James was tempted because he really needed the
money, and Mark was just an acquaintance. Or should he give some of it
to Mark, given that he was struggling? What should he do?

*[end of prompt --- copy everything between the two rules]*
--- STORY 2 ---

After weeks of intense preparation, Steve was thrilled to learn that his
team was awarded a performance bonus for exceeding their sales target.
The recognition felt satisfying---a tangible reward for the long hours
he'd poured into work and the many nights he'd stayed late fine-tuning
his pitch. The director called Steve to discuss the bonus and said:
"You guys did great. Since you are the team leader, the full bonus is
allocated to you. However, you may choose to give a portion to your
teammate Max if you wish. The final decision is yours." Now Steve faced
a choice. He could keep the full bonus, as initially allocated. Or he
could give some to Max, knowing that Max made a significant contribution
to the team's success. What should he do?

# Pairwise Ratings

**Game A × Story 1: 15**
The trust game involves multiplication of the transfer and a reciprocal return decision, neither of which is present in James's situation. James simply decides whether to share a windfall, with no strategic return expected.

**Game A × Story 2: 15**
Steve's decision is a one-shot allocation, not an investment with expected reciprocation. The multiplication and return-stage mechanics of the trust game have no analog in Steve's bonus-sharing scenario.

**Game B × Story 1: 15**
The ultimatum game gives the recipient veto power, which is absent in James's situation—Mark cannot reject or nullify James's decision. Only the "propose a split" element is loosely similar.

**Game B × Story 2: 15**
Max has no ability to reject the allocation or eliminate the payoff, so the strategic threat that defines the ultimatum game is missing. Steve's choice is unilateral.

**Game C × Story 1: 30**
Game C allows both giving and taking from a provisionally split allocation ($8/$4), whereas James's situation is closer to a pure dictator setup—Mark had nothing. The taking option in Game C doesn't match, though the free choice over a joint allocation is a partial parallel.

**Game C × Story 2: 30**
Similar reasoning: Max wasn't provisionally allocated anything, so the "take" option in Game C doesn't map to Steve's situation. The initial 8/4 split doesn't fit the 12/0 nature of the bonus allocation.

**Game D × Story 1: 85**
This is a near-perfect match: one party is fully allocated a resource ($12 vs. full aid), the other gets $0, and the allocated party can unilaterally choose how much (if any) to transfer. Only the framing (welfare windfall vs. lab endowment) differs.

**Game D × Story 2: 80**
Also a strong match—Steve holds the full endowment and can freely transfer any amount to Max. Slight difference: Max actually contributed to earning the bonus, introducing a desert/fairness consideration absent in the anonymous lab game.

---

{"ratings": {"A": {"Story 1": 15, "Story 2": 15}, "B": {"Story 1": 15, "Story 2": 15}, "C": {"Story 1": 30, "Story 2": 30}, "D": {"Story 1": 85, "Story 2": 80}}}

---

**Story 1** — Most similar: **Game D**, because it is a pure dictator setup with a 12/0 provisional allocation exactly mirroring James's exclusive receipt of aid. Least similar: **Games A and B (tied)**, since neither the multiplication/reciprocation of the trust game nor the veto structure of the ultimatum game appears in the story.

**Story 2** — Most similar: **Game D**, for the same reason—Steve holds the entire allocation and unilaterally decides whether to share, matching the dictator structure. Least similar: **Games A and B (tied)**, as Max has no ability to reject and there is no investment-return mechanism.

Now decompose your similarity judgments along explicit structural dimensions. For each of the four games (A, B, C, D) and each of the two stories (Story 1, Story 2) you analyzed above, specify the value on each of the following dimensions:

1. Pie structure: fixed-sum, or expandable through one player's action?

2. Player 1's initial endowment: full pie, or partial (recipient also gets a positive amount)?

3. Player 2's role: passive recipient, accept/reject responder, or reciprocator with a continuous choice?

4. Source of Player 1's endowment: earned through effort, awarded by selection or luck, produced through interaction, or unspecified?

5. Strategic structure: unilateral allocation, proposer-responder with veto, or sequential interaction with reciprocity?

OUTPUT FORMAT

1. Produce a table with six columns (A, B, C, D, Story 1, Story 2) and five rows (one per dimension). Fill each cell with the value on that dimension for that game or story.

2. Then answer these three questions explicitly:

(a) Which dimensions account for the largest similarity gaps in your Pass 1 ratings?

(b) Is any single dimension responsible for distinguishing one of the four games from the other three in its similarity to either story? If yes, name the dimension and the game.

(c) Does the answer to (b) differ across the two stories, or is it the same?

# Structural Decomposition Table

| Dimension | Game A | Game B | Game C | Game D | Story 1 | Story 2 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **1. Pie structure** | Expandable (×3 multiplier on transfer) | Fixed-sum ($12), but can collapse to $0 if rejected | Fixed-sum ($12) | Fixed-sum ($12) | Fixed-sum (aid amount) | Fixed-sum (bonus amount) |
| **2. P1's initial endowment** | Full pie ($6 vs $0) | Full pie ($12 vs $0) | Partial ($8 vs $4) | Full pie ($12 vs $0) | Full (James got all aid; Mark got $0) | Full (Steve got entire bonus; Max got $0) |
| **3. P2's role** | Reciprocator with continuous choice | Accept/reject responder (veto) | Passive recipient | Passive recipient | Passive recipient | Passive recipient |
| **4. Source of P1's endowment** | Unspecified (lab endowment) | Unspecified (lab endowment) | Unspecified (lab endowment) | Unspecified (lab endowment) | Awarded by selection (welfare agency chose James) | Earned through effort (team performance; Max also contributed) |
| **5. Strategic structure** | Sequential with reciprocity | Proposer-responder with veto | Unilateral allocation (with take option) | Unilateral allocation (give only) | Unilateral allocation | Unilateral allocation |

---

## (a) Which dimensions account for the largest similarity gaps in Pass 1?

The **strategic structure** (Dimension 5) and **Player 2's role** (Dimension 3) drove the biggest gaps. Both stories feature purely unilateral allocations with a passive recipient, so games with reciprocity (A) or veto power (B) scored much lower than the pure dictator games (C, D). Secondarily, **Player 1's initial endowment** (Dimension 2) separated Game C from Game D: the 8/4 split in C is a weaker match to the stories' full-endowment structure than D's 12/0 split.

## (b) Does any single dimension distinguish one game from the other three?

Yes—actually two cases:

- **Dimension 3 (P2's role) / Dimension 5 (strategic structure)** jointly distinguish **Game A** from B, C, D: only A has an active reciprocator and an expandable pie. This makes A structurally the furthest from either story's unilateral logic.
- **Dimension 2 (P1's endowment)** distinguishes **Game C** from A, B, D: only C starts with a partial (8/4) split rather than a full endowment to P1. This is what pushes C below D in similarity to both stories, even though C and D share the same unilateral structure.

Game D stands out as uniquely matching the stories on *all* structural dimensions except the source of endowment.

## (c) Does this differ across the two stories?

**Essentially the same** for both stories. The ranking D > C > A ≈ B holds in both cases, driven by the same structural features (unilateral allocation, full endowment to P1, passive recipient). The one dimension that differs meaningfully between the stories is **Dimension 4 (source of endowment)**: Story 1 involves luck/selection while Story 2 involves earned effort with a contributing teammate. This introduces a desert/fairness consideration in Story 2 that none of the four games capture, but since all four games are equally silent on this dimension, it doesn't change the *relative* ranking of games within each story—it only slightly lowers D's absolute score for Story 2 (80 vs 85).

Now consider the reverse retrieval direction. For each of the four games (A, B, C, D), imagine a participant who has just read the game instructions for the first time and is asked: "Does this situation remind you of any real-world experience?"

Of the two stories (Story 1 and Story 2), which is more likely to be retrieved as a similar past experience cued by each game?

For each game, distribute 100 points between Story 1 and Story 2 to indicate relative retrieval likelihood. For example, 70/30 means Story 1 is much more likely to come to mind than Story 2 when cued by that game; 50/50 means equal likelihood.

OUTPUT FORMAT

1. For each game, give the 100-point split (Story 1 / Story 2) and a 2-3 sentence justification.

2. At the end, output a single JSON object with the splits, exactly in this form:
{"splits": {"A": {"Story 1": <int>, "Story 2": <int>}, "B": {...}, "C": {...}, "D": {...}}}
Each game's two numbers must sum to 100.

3. After the JSON, comment briefly on whether the relative-retrieval ranking across games matches your Pass 1 absolute similarity ratings, or differs (and if so, where and why).

# Reverse Retrieval Analysis

**Game A (Trust Game): 40 / 60**
Neither story matches well since neither involves reciprocation or an investment mechanism. Story 2 pulls slightly ahead because the workplace context involves an ongoing relationship where reciprocity/reputation could plausibly matter (Max might reciprocate future favors), while James and Mark are mere acquaintances with no expected return.

**Game B (Ultimatum Game): 45 / 55**
Neither story features veto power, so retrieval is weak either way. Story 2 edges ahead because the workplace bonus involves a co-contributor (Max) who could plausibly react negatively or push back, mildly evoking the responder role; James's neighbor has no such standing over the welfare aid.

**Game C (Take-or-Give with partial allocation): 60 / 40**
The initial partial allocation (8/4) suggests a shared-pool situation where both parties have some claim. Story 1 fits slightly better because welfare aid is drawn from a common government pool with multiple applicants having claims, evoking distributive-justice framing. Story 2's bonus was allocated entirely to Steve, so the "take from other" option feels less natural.

**Game D (Dictator Game): 50 / 50**
Both stories are near-perfect matches for the dictator structure—one party gets the full endowment and can freely share. Story 1 matches on the "selected/lucky" framing (windfall); Story 2 matches on the "workplace allocation with contributor" framing. Retrieval is roughly balanced, with either story easily coming to mind.

---

{"splits": {"A": {"Story 1": 40, "Story 2": 60}, "B": {"Story 1": 45, "Story 2": 55}, "C": {"Story 1": 60, "Story 2": 40}, "D": {"Story 1": 50, "Story 2": 50}}}

---

## Comparison with Pass 1 Absolute Similarity Ratings

The retrieval rankings **partially diverge** from the Pass 1 absolute similarity ratings, in informative ways:

- **Consistent**: Game D remains the strongest match for both stories in absolute terms, and retrieval is balanced (both stories come to mind readily). This aligns with Pass 1's near-tied high scores (85/80).

- **Divergent for Games A and B**: In Pass 1, I rated both stories equally low (15/15) against these games because neither story matches the reciprocity or veto structure. But in *relative* retrieval, Story 2 pulls ahead because its workplace/ongoing-relationship context weakly evokes reciprocity and accountability cues that Story 1's one-shot neighbor encounter lacks. Absolute similarity was low but *equal*; relative retrieval breaks the tie via surface/contextual cues.

- **Divergent for Game C**: Pass 1 rated both stories equally (30/30) against C, but retrieval favors Story 1 because welfare aid naturally evokes a shared-pool/multiple-claimants schema matching the 8/4 partial allocation, whereas Steve's bonus was clearly his alone.

The general pattern: when absolute similarity is high and matched (Game D), retrieval is balanced; when absolute similarity is low and tied (Games A, B, C), *secondary surface features* (workplace relationship, shared-pool framing) drive the retrieval split even though they didn't move the structural-similarity needle much in Pass 1.
